name: Redirect Doctor
author: Frederic_LEGUEN

sections.description:
You have been redirecting URLs for years. Every rename, every restructure, every fixed typo
added one more rule. Nobody ever went back to check whether they still make sense together.

Redirect Doctor reads the redirects you already have and tells you what is wrong with them.

It does not create redirects behind your back and it does not replace your redirection plugin.
It works with Redirection, Rank Math and Yoast SEO Premium, and audits what is there,
on ten screens:

  • Chained redirects — /a/ sends to /b/, which sends to /c/. Every visitor and every
    search engine pays for the extra hops. Cascades of eight steps are common on old sites.
  • Loops — /a/ sends to /b/, and /b/ sends back to /a/. The browser gives up and the
    page never opens. This is the only fault that truly breaks something for a visitor.
  • Conflicts — the same address with two different destinations. Only one can win, and it is
    not always the one you meant.
  • Duplicates — the same rule written several times over the years.
  • 404 errors, grouped — not a raw log, but pages people actually keep asking for, sorted by
    how often they are hit, with a suggested destination for each.
  • Redirects safe to delete — rules that have not sent a single visitor in years.
  • Redirects sent to the home page — rules that do not send the visitor to a replacement
    page, but to your home page. This is not a redirect, it is a soft 404: you are telling
    Google that a dead address now holds your home page, and your home page slowly takes on the
    reputation of every dead address pointed at it.
  • Doubtful destinations — redirects whose starting address and destination share no word
    at all. Often a batch of rules pointed at something that has nothing to do with them. The
    screen ranks them; you decide, and you can mark a pair as intended so it stops being
    reported.
  • Links to fix in your content — posts and pages that still link to an address which now
    redirects. Fixing the link removes the hop at the source.
  • Redirects in .htaccess — the redirects written in your .htaccess file, shown for
    information whatever plugin you use. The server reads that file before WordPress, so a rule
    there wins over any plugin. Redirect Doctor reads it and never modifies it.

Everything is measured against your own site. No external service is contacted, no data leaves
your server, and nothing is written unless you tick a box and click a button.

Works with Redirection, Rank Math and Yoast SEO Premium

Redirect Doctor reads the redirects of Redirection (John Godley), of the Rank Math
Redirections module, and of Yoast SEO Premium — including the rules Yoast leaves behind in
your database after it has been uninstalled.

It works on one plugin at a time. If several of them hold redirects on your site, it stops
and asks you which one is the reference: correcting the wrong one would repair nothing.

Yoast keeps neither a hit counter, nor a date of last use, nor a 404 log. The two screens that
need them say so instead of showing empty or misleading figures.

If no redirect plugin is active, Redirect Doctor tells you so and has nothing to analyse.

What the free version does

The free version is a complete diagnosis. All ten screens, the real totals, the filters,
the search, the CSV export, the copy-to-clipboard button — and the printable health check.

That health check sums up everything found on your site in numbers, with the risk each one
represents, and names no address. You can hand it to a client or a manager as it is.

Each table shows its first five rows, and tells you how many more there are. The counters on
the tiles are never rounded, never capped and never faked: if your site has 1,609 unresolved
404s, it says 1,609.

Two things belong to the Pro version:

  1. Fixing. Every action button is visible but switched off. Nothing is deleted, created or
    rewritten by the free version — ever.
  2. The addresses that form your loops. The free version tells you how many loops you have
    and how many redirects they involve. Finding a loop buried in fifteen years of accumulated
    rules is the hard part; undoing it takes three clicks.

What the Pro version adds

  • Every row of every table, not the first five.
  • The loop map: which addresses point at each other.
  • One-click fixing, with an undo. Shorten a chain so each step goes straight to the final
    destination. Delete dead rules. Create redirects for your most-hit 404s. Break a loop by
    removing a link.
  • Rewriting the links inside your content that still point at an old address, as relative
    addresses so they survive a domain change.
  • Importing from one plugin to another. Bring the redirects of an old plugin, or of your
    .htaccess file, into the plugin you use: identical rules are left out, missing ones are ticked
    one by one, and leftovers can be deleted from the old plugin. Every step can be undone.
  • An action log of everything that was changed, with its own export.
  • A health check that also shows where you started and where you are now.

Nothing is ever changed without a ticked box, and every batch stays recoverable afterwards.

Pro is available from orion-sigma.com.
sections.installation:
1. Make sure Redirection, Rank Math (with its Redirections module) or Yoast SEO Premium
    is installed and active — Redirect Doctor reads their data.
  2. Upload the redirect-doctor folder to /wp-content/plugins/, or install the ZIP from
    Plugins → Add New → Upload Plugin.
  3. Activate the plugin.
  4. Open Tools → Redirect Doctor. The first analysis runs on its own.

The analysis re-runs by itself once a week, and immediately after any change you make.
sections.faq:
Does it change anything on my site by itself?

No. The free version writes nothing at all — the code that writes is not even included in the
free download. In the Pro version, nothing happens without a ticked box and a click, and every
batch you delete stays recoverable.

Will it slow my site down?

No. Everything happens in the WordPress admin, on demand. Nothing is added to the pages your
visitors see.

Which redirect plugins does it work with?

Redirection, Rank Math and Yoast SEO Premium. Redirects written in your .htaccess file are read
too, and shown for information. Your host’s redirect manager is not read.

Does it modify my .htaccess file?

No, never. Redirect Doctor only reads it. When a redirect exists both in the .htaccess file and
in your plugin, it tells you which line to remove by hand.

What is a redirect chain, and why should I care?

/old-page/ sends to /newer-page/, which sends to /current-page/. The visitor’s browser
makes three requests instead of one, and search engines dilute the signal at every hop. Pointing
each rule straight at the final destination fixes it without breaking any of the old addresses.

Why does the free version hide which addresses form my loops?

Because on that one screen, knowing is the work. Once you know that /a/ and /b/ point at
each other, removing one of them takes three clicks. Spotting that pair inside years of
accumulated rules is what the plugin is for. Every other screen shows you real rows from your
own site.

Is my data sent anywhere?

No. Redirect Doctor contacts no external service. Everything it reads and writes stays in your
own database.

In which languages is it available?

English and French. Translations live in /languages/ and can be edited with any translation
plugin.
sections.changelog:
4.5.2

  • Main screen: a clear dashboard at the top (last analysis, duration, redirects scanned), with a small button to run the analysis again.
  • Information about which plugins hold redirect rules now lives in Settings. Real warnings (no tool running, two tools in conflict) stay on the main screen.
  • Free version: a notice on the plugin screen explains what the Pro version adds.

4.3.2

  • 404 errors: an address marked as gone (410) now leaves the list right away.

4.3.1

  • 404 errors: a missing file (renamed or resized image) can now be redirected to the right file.

4.3.0

  • 404 errors: new button Mark as gone (410). The address answers 410 Gone, so search engines drop it
    instead of coming back to it. For robots, old tags and addresses that will never return.

4.2.3

  • New tab Dead destinations: redirects whose final destination is not a real page. Each path is
    followed to the end, whichever plugin carries each step. Pro: redirect them elsewhere, or delete them.

4.1.0

  • Duplicates and Conflicts: the rule marked Kept is now the one with the most hits, not the
    first in the list. A rule created recently no longer hides the one your visitors really use.

4.0.8

  • Import: the box at the top of a table now ticks the rows of that table only.

4.0.7

  • Import now moves the redirects: once imported, they are deleted from the old plugin.
    “Undo the import” puts them back there.

4.0.6

  • Import: the counter at the top now adds up exactly the rows of the tables shown below.

4.0.5

  • Import: addresses that WordPress already redirects by itself (the old address of a post whose address changed) are no longer offered for import.

4.0.2

  • .htaccess: rules whose destination depends on the address requested ($1, $2…) are shown apart, as written, and no longer counted or listed as page redirects.

4.0.1

  • Pro: the Licence screen opens again. It called a function removed in 3.3.1.

4.0.0

  • Redirect Doctor is no longer limited to Redirection: it now reads and fixes the redirects
    of Rank Math and Yoast SEO Premium too. Redirection is no longer required.
  • A new Settings screen: when several plugins hold redirects, you choose the one Redirect
    Doctor works on. The others are never touched.
  • A tenth screen lists the redirects of your .htaccess file, for information. Redirect Doctor
    never modifies that file. A rule present both there and in your plugin shows up in
    Duplicates or Conflicts, with the line to remove by hand.
  • Doubtful destinations: three buttons on one line — delete, apply a 410, or mark as intended.
  • Pro: import redirects from another plugin or from .htaccess into the plugin you use, and
    delete the leftovers from the old one. Every step can be undone.
  • Rank Math: 404 errors are read when its 404 Monitor module is on, and the screen says so
    when it is off.
  • Yoast keeps no hits, dates or 404 log: the screens that need them say so.

3.3.3

  • New colour for the main action button.

3.3.2

  • The target address now keeps its trailing slash on screen and, above all, in the links
    that “Links to fix” rewrites. Writing /page instead of /page/ made WordPress answer with
    a canonical redirect, so the tool replaced one pointless round trip with another.
  • The rewritten link is taken from the canonical permalink of the destination when the
    destination is a published post or page.

3.3.1

  • Inline CSS and JS now go through the official WordPress functions: wp_register_style with
    wp_add_inline_style for the admin screens, wp_print_inline_style_tag and
    wp_print_inline_script_tag for the standalone report.
  • The print button no longer carries an inline onclick handler.

3.3.0

  • Renamed to Redirect Doctor. The former name was the registered trademark of an unrelated company.
  • New menu icon: a stethoscope drawn in the plugin, as no Dashicon suggests health.

3.2.4

  • Reads a third form of destination used by Redirection for “URL and server” rules,
    where the target sits inside a serialised array. The report showed that raw array instead
    of the address.
  • Shortening a chain now writes inside that form instead of replacing it, so the rule keeps
    its server and its fallback address. Replacing it would have broken the rule.

3.2.3

  • First release on WordPress.org.
  • Nine screens, laid out vertically: chained redirects, loops, conflicts, duplicates, grouped
    404s, redirects sent to the home page, doubtful destinations, redirects safe to delete, and
    links to fix inside your own content.
  • Doubtful destinations: compares the words of a starting address with those of its
    destination, and lets you mark a pair as intended so it stops being reported.
  • Detects a site redirecting to itself in an endless loop, and recognises the WooCommerce
    geolocation fingerprint behind it.
  • A one-click health check, ready to print or save as PDF. It names no address, so it can be
    handed to a client as it is.

2.32.0

  • New, and free: spots addresses that are not missing pages at all, but a site redirecting to
    itself in an endless loop. Names the culprit when your server reports it.
  • Recognises the WooCommerce geolocation fingerprint, and says exactly which setting to change.

2.31.0

  • Pro: rewrite the links inside your content that still point at an old address. Tick the lines,
    click once, and undo it if you change your mind.
  • Links are written as relative addresses, so they survive a domain change.

2.30.0

  • Pro: a Licence screen. Enter your key, the site is registered, the fixing features open.
  • If our licence server is ever unreachable, nothing changes on your site.

2.28.0

  • New: a one-click health check, ready to print or save as PDF. It sums up the whole analysis
    in numbers and names no address, so it can be handed to a client as it is.
  • Pro: the report also shows where you started and where you are now.

2.27.0

  • Declares Redirection as a required plugin, so WordPress refuses activation without it instead of showing an empty screen.
  • Added this readme.

2.26.0

  • The “more rows” notice is now the last row of the table, introduced by three dots, instead of
    a paragraph underneath. A table that stops dead looks complete.
  • The CSV export skips that row.

2.25.0

  • The free version shows the first five rows of each table, and says how many remain. Five per
    table, not per screen. Tile counters remain complete and truthful.

2.24.0

  • The loops screen now reports how many loops exist and how many redirects they involve, without
    listing the addresses, in the free version.

2.23.0

  • Free and Pro became two separate downloads. The code that writes to the database now lives in
    its own file, which the free package does not contain.

2.22.0

  • Conflicts split away from duplicates: the same address with two different destinations is a
    far more serious fault than a rule written twice.
  • Nine screens, each with its own colour, and an explanation written in plain language.

2.16.0

  • Action history, with its own export.
  • Deleting a batch became recoverable.

short_description: A health check for the redirects you already have, in Redirection, Rank Math or Yoast: chains, loops, conflicts, duplicates and 404s.

upgrade_notice.4.0.0: Redirect Doctor now works with Rank Math and Yoast SEO Premium as well as Redirection, which is no longer required. If several plugins hold redirects, choose your reference in Settings.
upgrade_notice.2.23.0: Free and Pro are now two separate downloads. If you own the Pro version, install the Pro ZIP — installing the free one removes the fixing features.

screenshots.caption: The nine tiles, each with the real count of what was found, and the redirect chains below: every cascade on one row, from the first address to the page that actually opens.
Loops. Address A points to B, B points back to A, and the page never opens. This is the only fault on the whole plugin that truly breaks something for a visitor.
Conflicting addresses: the same address with several rules leading to different places. Only one ever fires, and the Last use column says which.
Duplicates: the same rule written several times over the years.
Missing pages, grouped by address and counted instead of stacked one line per hit, with the Kind column separating real visitors from robots and missing files. The free version lists the first five.
Redirects sent to the home page. Not a redirect, a soft 404 — and the screen says what to do about it. The free version lists the first five.
Doubtful destinations: redirects whose start and destination share no word at all. Ranked, filterable, and a pair can be marked as intended.
Redirects safe to delete, split between never used and unused for over three years.
Links to fix inside your own content: posts and pages still pointing at an address that now redirects. Fixing the link removes the hop at the source.
